lines.trans: Wake up, Lyova, we have an inspection!
Chef, the inspector is already entering the hall!
Quickly clear everything extra off the tables.
Where to hide these old products?
Carry all this straight into the refrigerator.
And what to do with dirty aprons?
Lyova, immediately throw them into the wash!
I already sent Senya for cloths.
Wipe the floor, it is too slippery!
The cooks are already washing their workstations.
The kitchen must be ideally clean!
We will manage to do everything in time, chef!
To your stations, the inspector is already here!

Quickly clear everything extra off the tables.
Lyova, immediately throw them into the wash!
Wipe the floor, it is too slippery!

Today will be a very difficult day.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to throw', forming an aspectual pair with 'бросить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to leave, to abandon') (бросать трубку = to hang up) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Он всегда бросает вещи на пол.
examples.trans: He always throws things on the floor.

examples.text: Не бросайте трубку, умоляю вас! Я перед вами стою на коленях.
examples.trans: Don't hang up, I'm begging you! I'm on my knees in front of you.

meanings.note: the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order
the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

examples.text: Давай работай быстрее, гости уже давно ждут заказ!
examples.trans: Come on, work faster, the guests have been waiting for their order for a long time!

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

вовремя.gloss: on time, at the right moment

meanings.en: on time, at the right moment
meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'on time'.

examples.text: Ну как же ты не вовремя! Где ты сейчас?
examples.trans: Your timing couldn't be worse! Where are you now?

meanings.note: ends a conversation or an order: 'Всё, свободен' = that's all, you can go
Secondary conversational sense ('that's it, done') (at the start of a sentence) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'тереть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to wipe', forming an aspectual pair with 'вытирать'.

examples.text: Когда не можешь сам себе нос вытереть.
examples.trans: When you can't even wipe your own nose yourself.
Wipe your hands with a towel.

examples.text: Я уже вытерла слёзы и готова.
examples.trans: I already dried my tears and am ready.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('dirty').

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to make') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: + infinitive; agrees with the subject: должна (f)
Secondary conversational sense ('owe') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Жадность, Паша, должна быть умеренная. Комнатной температуры.
examples.trans: Greed, Pasha, should be moderate. Room temperature.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Declinable masculine noun meaning 'hall', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('living room') (regional/colloquial) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Understood. And who is managing the dining room?

заходить.gloss: to come in, to drop in

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'ходить'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to come in', forming an aspectual pair with 'зайти'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to drop in') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Не стой в дверях, смелее заходи ко мне в кабинет!
examples.trans: Do not stand in the doorway, come on into my office boldly!

examples.text: После работы мы часто заходим выпить кофе в соседний бар.
examples.trans: After work we often drop in to drink coffee at the neighboring bar.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.
Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'ideally'.

examples.trans: The kitchen must be ideally clean!

meanings.note: From Latin 'inspector' (observer, overseer, from 'inspicere', to look into).

examples.trans: The inspector is checking the kitchen.

examples.text: Инспекторы ищут нарушения только ради денег.
examples.trans: Inspectors look for violations only for money.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'where'.

examples.trans: Wait, where are you two going?

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'extra' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('unnecessary, too much') (сказать лишнего = to say too much) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Yesterday I said too much to you.
Do you have a spare ticket?
The main thing is do not say unnecessary foolishness.

meanings.note: in 'рабочее место' = workplace, job
Secondary conversational sense ('post, position') (на его место = in his place) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to wash', forming an aspectual pair with 'помыть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Юля, встала и пошла мыть посуду!
examples.trans: Yulia, get up and go wash the dishes!

examples.text: Пока ещё на мои деньги куплен! Встала и мыть посуду, шагом марш!
examples.trans: It's still bought with my money! Get up and wash the dishes, forward march!

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'медленно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
one direction, now; 'Неси!' = Bring (it)!

examples.trans: Yulia, bring a pen and a piece of paper.

meanings.note: accusative/genitive его (него after prepositions), dative ему (нему)
Secondary conversational sense ('it') (for masculine and neuter things) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
High-frequency Russian pronoun ('they') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.en: to send (a person, a letter, a message)
meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'править'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to send', paired with 'отправлять'.

examples.text: И бабушку на лечение в Израиль отправил.
examples.trans: And he sent our grandmother to Israel for treatment.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'along' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('along, around') (+ dative) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('by (phone)') ('по телефону') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Это Аракелян. Я по поводу торгового центра.
examples.trans: It's Arakelyan. I'm calling about the shopping centre.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cook', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'floor', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'верка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'check, inspection, test' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: An inspection is underway at the bank.

examples.text: Эксперты уже начали проверку состояния старой стены.
examples.trans: Experts have already begun checking the condition of the old wall.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'дукт'). Common masculine noun meaning 'product, foodstuff' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Ты будешь целый день разгружать продукты!
examples.trans: You will unload groceries the whole day!
The guests need the freshest product!

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'straight'.
Secondary conversational sense ('straight ahead') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: В смысле, Виктор Степанович? Прямо так, да?
examples.trans: What do you mean, Viktor Stepanovich? Just like that?

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'working', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('worker') (as a noun) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы построим кластер. Это тысячи рабочих мест.
examples.trans: We will build the cluster. That means thousands of jobs.

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: refers back to the subject: 'он держит своё слово' = he keeps his word

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'делать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to do', forming an aspectual pair with 'делать'.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'кользкий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('slippery').

examples.trans: The floor in the kitchen is very slippery.
Wipe the floor, it is too slippery!
A slippery floor is a source of danger.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лишком').

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'пать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to sleep', paired with 'поспать'.

examples.text: Ладно, утром позвоню ей. Поехали спать.
examples.trans: All right, I'll call her in the morning. Let's go to sleep.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'прятать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to hide', paired with 'прятать'.

examples.text: Мэр куда-то спрятал деньги. Местные чиновники не могут собрать нужную сумму.
examples.trans: The mayor has hidden the money somewhere. The local officials can't put together the sum they need.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'old', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('former, old') ('старый друг' = an old friend) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Славик, смотри сюда. Меняю свой новый айфон на твой старый телефон.
examples.trans: Slavik, look here. I'll swap my new iPhone for your old phone.

meanings.note: начать со стирки = start with the laundry

examples.trans: We'll start with the laundry. Let's go.

examples.text: Лёва, немедленно бросай их в стирку!
examples.trans: Lyova, immediately throw them into the wash!

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'table', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: We will sit together in a friendly way at the table.

examples.text: Не бойся, всё в порядке! Посидим дружно за столом.
examples.trans: Don't be afraid, everything is fine! We will sit together in a friendly way at the table.
Take your feet off the table quickly!

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('difficult, hard').

examples.text: Детство у меня было трудное. Я вырос в коммуналке.
examples.trans: My childhood was hard. I grew up in a communal flat.

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'rag'.
Secondary conversational sense ('pushover, spineless person (colloq.)') (used of either a man or a woman) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Если он тряпка, то я нет.
examples.trans: If he's a pushover, I'm not.

examples.text: Послушай ты, очкарик! Если он тряпка, то я нет.
examples.trans: Listen here, four-eyes! If he's a pushover, I'm not.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'бирать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to clean up, to tidy', paired with 'убрать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to put away') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже не могу готовить, стирать, убирать. Я хочу на море!
examples.trans: I can't take the cooking, washing and cleaning any more. I want to go to the sea!

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.

успеть.gloss: to make it, to be in time

meanings.en: to make it, to be in time
meanings.note: + на: успеть на поезд = catch the train
Secondary conversational sense ('to manage to do') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: We'll make it! The president always talks for a long time.

examples.text: Если будем работать дружно, мы обязательно успеем к началу ужина!
examples.trans: If we work together harmoniously, we will definitely make it in time for dinner!

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'apron', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: А что делать с грязными фартуками?
examples.trans: And what to do with dirty aprons?

examples.text: Я просто принёс чистые поварские фартуки.
examples.trans: I just brought clean chef aprons.

meanings.note: Derived noun with agent/object suffix '-ник'/'-щик'/'-чик'. Common masculine noun meaning 'fridge' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The milk is in the fridge.

examples.text: Курица? Нет. А чей это холодильник?
examples.trans: Chicken? No. And whose fridge is this?

meanings.note: short form чисто: всё чисто = everything is clean
Secondary conversational sense ('pure') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Нин, я всё помыл. Всё чисто.
examples.trans: Nina, I washed everything. It's all clean.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
